brief.situation: 15:00 in the PICU. You are the nurse for Ava, 11 years old, 38 kg, intubated after a bicycle crash this morning with a severe traumatic brain injury. She has an intracranial pressure (ICP) monitor and an arterial line; she is sedated on infusions as ordered. Her cervical spine has not been cleared.
handover: Her ICP has run 12-16 mmHg all day. The neurosurgeon is in the hospital.
Physical therapy just repositioned her flat to change her linen, and her head is turned to the right on a rolled towel.

Unit TBI protocol: head of bed 30 degrees with the head midline and the collar fitted, avoid hypotension, hypoxia and fever, target normal CO2, keep the cerebral perfusion pressure at or above 40 mmHg; the nurse calls the intensivist and neurosurgeon at once for an ICP of 20 or more for 5 minutes; hyperosmolar therapy is given on order.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Why has Ava's ICP risen, and what do you do?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: An ICP of 20 or more for over 5 minutes is intracranial hypertension; lying flat with the head turned and a tight collar impede venous drainage; CPP must stay at or above 40.
parts.modelAnswer: Her ICP has been over 20 for six minutes since she was laid flat with her head turned and the collar tight, which blocks venous drainage. Her CPP is heading down toward 40.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Puts the head of bed at 30 degrees with the head midline and the collar refitted, minimizes stimulation, keeps normal CO2 without hyperventilating, and calls the intensivist and neurosurgeon at once.
parts.modelAnswer: Head up to 30, midline, fix the collar, keep things quiet, keep her CO2 normal, and call the intensivist and neurosurgeon now. No hyperventilating.

herniation.headline: Herniation signs
herniation.body: A sustained ICP of 20 or more needs the protocol's first steps (head up, midline, collar loose, normal CO2) and the team at once. Never hyperventilate prophylactically.

safe.body: You read the trend, fixed the positioning and collar, kept normal CO2 and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

scoring.modelReasoning: In pediatric severe TBI, an ICP of 20 mmHg or more is treated and CPP is kept at or above 40 mmHg. Ava's rise followed flat positioning with her head turned and a tight collar, which obstruct venous drainage: put the head of bed at 30 degrees, head midline, collar refitted, cluster care, keep normal CO2, and call the intensivist and neurosurgeon at once for hyperosmolar therapy and imaging. Prophylactic severe hyperventilation (PaCO2 under 30) in the first 48 hours is not suggested; it lowers ICP by cutting cerebral blood flow.
